questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q01

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

A student is preparing a memoir excerpt for digital publication. Which first step best matches the lesson process?

answer.text: A. Identify the genre and decide what the reader needs to see clearly.

feedback.text: Correct. Publication formatting begins with genre and reader needs.

answer.text: B. Add decorative symbols before every paragraph.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Decoration is not the first step and may distract from readability.

answer.text: C. Delete the title to save space.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A title helps prepare the reader. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: D. Submit the first draft without previewing it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A publication-ready file needs a final check.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q02

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which choice best improves readability in a prose scene?

answer.text: A. Put dialogue from three speakers in one paragraph.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This makes the scene difficult to follow.

answer.text: B. Remove paragraph breaks because they are optional.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Paragraph breaks guide readers through action and dialogue.

answer.text: C. Start a new paragraph when a new speaker talks.

feedback.text: Correct. This helps readers track speaker changes. This answer matches the lesson skill and is supported by the specific creative-writing evidence in the prompt.

answer.text: D. Add random blank lines after every word.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Random spacing creates confusion. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q03

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

A poem's line breaks were copied incorrectly into one paragraph. What should the writer do?

answer.text: A. Turn the poem into a script.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The genre does not need to change.

answer.text: B. Add unrelated images to fill the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Extra content does not solve a formatting problem.

answer.text: C. Remove all white space forever.

feedback.text: Incorrect. White space can be meaningful in poetry.

answer.text: D. Restore purposeful line breaks and stanza breaks from the revised poem.

feedback.text: Correct. Line and stanza breaks are part of the poem's meaning and pacing.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q04

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which file-readiness action is strongest?

answer.text: A. Keep bracketed notes that say fix later.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Draft notes make the piece look unfinished.

answer.text: B. Use a clear file name, preview the file, and remove draft comments.

feedback.text: Correct. These steps prepare the piece for a reader or LMS submission.

answer.text: C. Submit several versions so the reader can choose.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The assignment asks for the final version unless drafts are requested.

answer.text: D. Ignore the file name.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Clear file naming supports organization and submission.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q05

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

A student says, "I made the font bright because publication should look exciting." What is the best feedback?

answer.text: A. Correct, because bright color always improves writing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Visual excitement does not automatically improve readability.

answer.text: B. Correct, because conventions no longer matter online.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital publication still requires readable conventions. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: C. Incorrect, because formatting should support genre, readability, and audience access.

feedback.text: Correct. Publication formatting is purposeful, not random decoration.

answer.text: D. Incorrect, because all creative work must use plain text only.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The issue is not all visual choice; the issue is whether the choice supports the reader.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q06

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which question belongs in a digital readability check?

answer.text: A. Does every break, label, or paragraph help the reader follow the piece?

feedback.text: Correct. This directly checks whether formatting choices support readability.

answer.text: B. Is the piece impossible to revise?

feedback.text: Incorrect. The check is about reader access, not giving up revision.

answer.text: C. Did the writer choose the longest possible title?

feedback.text: Incorrect. A title should be clear, not automatically long.

answer.text: D. Can the reader guess missing context?

feedback.text: Incorrect. A reader-ready piece should not rely on guessing.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q07

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

A script draft has stage directions mixed into spoken dialogue. What revision best supports the reader?

answer.text: A. Remove all stage directions from the play.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Stage directions can be useful when clearly formatted.

answer.text: B. Add a title but leave the dialogue confusing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The title alone does not fix the script format problem.

answer.text: C. Replace all character names with initials without explanation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That may make the script harder to follow.

answer.text: D. Format stage directions consistently so they do not look like spoken lines.

feedback.text: Correct. This helps the reader distinguish action from dialogue.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q08

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which publication note is strongest?

answer.text: A. I submitted it because I was finished.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This does not explain any format choice.

answer.text: B. I used stanza breaks to separate the three image groups so the reader can follow the poem's movement.

feedback.text: Correct. This names the formatting choice and explains reader effect.

answer.text: C. I changed things randomly until it looked different.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Publication formatting must be purposeful. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: D. I used a bright font because readers like color.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This does not connect format to genre or meaning.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q09

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

What is the purpose of previewing a file before submission?

answer.text: A. To avoid reading the piece again.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Previewing is a form of careful rereading.

answer.text: B. To add more draft comments.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Draft comments should usually be removed from the final version.

answer.text: C. To see the piece the way a reader will see it.

feedback.text: Correct. Previewing helps catch spacing, format, and readability problems.

answer.text: D. To change the genre at the last minute.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Previewing checks presentation, not genre replacement. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q10

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which choice best describes format-specific quality work?

answer.text: A. Every genre uses exactly the same format.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Different genres have different reader needs. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: B. The writer adds as many visual effects as possible.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Effects that distract from reading weaken publication quality.

answer.text: C. The file name is left blank.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A clear file name supports readiness. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: D. The piece is formatted so its genre is clear and readable.

feedback.text: Correct. Format-specific quality means the final form supports the kind of writing.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q11

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

A student includes a note at the top that says "rough version, maybe final." What should happen before submission?

answer.text: A. Remove the draft label and submit a clearly final version.

feedback.text: Correct. The reader should receive the intended final version.

answer.text: B. Leave it because it is honest.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A final publication version should not include confusing draft labels.

answer.text: C. Add more uncertain notes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. More draft notes make the piece less ready.

answer.text: D. Hide the title instead.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The title should stay clear. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q12

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which conventions pass is most appropriate for a final publication version?

answer.text: A. Rewrite the entire piece into a new topic.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A conventions pass is not a full replacement of meaning.

answer.text: B. Ignore dialogue punctuation because it is creative writing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dialogue punctuation helps readers understand speech. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: C. Check capitalization, punctuation, spelling, and paragraphing without changing intentional style.

feedback.text: Correct. This removes distracting errors while preserving creative choices.

answer.text: D. Add misspellings to make the piece unique.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Accidental errors distract readers. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q13

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which answer best explains why a title matters in digital publication?

answer.text: A. A title replaces the need for formatting.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The piece still needs readable format. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: B. A title can prepare the reader and make the piece look complete.

feedback.text: Correct. A clear title gives the reader an entry point.

answer.text: C. A title should always reveal the ending.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Titles do not have to spoil the piece.

answer.text: D. A title is only needed for research papers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Creative writing pieces often need titles too.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q14

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

A writer uses different spacing styles for each character label in a script. What problem does this create?

answer.text: A. It makes the script too poetic.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The problem is not poetry; it is inconsistent readability.

answer.text: B. It automatically improves performance.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inconsistency usually makes performance harder. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: C. It removes the need for stage directions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Labels and stage directions serve different purposes.

answer.text: D. It can confuse readers about who is speaking and how the scene is organized.

feedback.text: Correct. Consistent labels support script clarity. This answer matches the lesson skill and is supported by the specific creative-writing evidence in the prompt.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q15

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which action best prepares a portfolio piece for online collaborative publication?

answer.text: A. Check that the final version is clear, complete, readable, and named correctly.

feedback.text: Correct. These qualities support online publication readiness. This answer matches the lesson skill and is supported by the specific creative-writing evidence in the prompt.

answer.text: B. Submit a version with unresolved comments.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unresolved comments can confuse readers unless process evidence is requested.

answer.text: C. Use unclear labels so readers ask questions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Publication should reduce unnecessary confusion. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: D. Remove all formatting from every genre.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Genre-specific formatting is part of quality.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q16

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Why should a writer remove placeholder labels such as "fix this later"?

answer.text: A. They prove the writer revised carefully.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Leftover labels suggest the final pass was incomplete.

answer.text: B. They are required in every final draft.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Final drafts should usually remove drafting labels.

answer.text: C. They make the piece look unfinished and distract the reader.

feedback.text: Correct. Final publication should not include accidental drafting reminders.

answer.text: D. They replace the need for a publication note.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A publication note explains choices; placeholders show unfinished work.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q17

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which sentence best distinguishes formatting from decoration?

answer.text: A. Formatting means adding unrelated pictures.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That describes decoration, not necessarily useful format.

answer.text: B. Formatting supports readability and genre; decoration may be visual but not always useful.

feedback.text: Correct. Purposeful formatting helps the reader, while decoration can distract.

answer.text: C. Decoration always improves publication quality.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Decoration can weaken readability. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: D. Formatting is only about making text smaller.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Formatting includes title, spacing, breaks, labels, and order.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q18

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which example shows a reader-ready opening?

answer.text: A. No title, no author label, and a draft note.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These features make the piece look unfinished.

answer.text: B. Random blank lines before the first sentence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Random spacing can confuse readers. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: C. A warning that the writer did not proofread.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Final publication should be proofread. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: D. A clear title, clean first paragraph, and no leftover drafting comments.

feedback.text: Correct. These choices prepare the reader to enter the piece.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q19

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

A student says, "I cannot change any spacing because the words are already revised." What is the best response?

answer.text: A. Spacing is part of publication readiness and can be revised without changing meaning.

feedback.text: Correct. Formatting changes can improve reader access while preserving content.

answer.text: B. Spacing never matters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Spacing affects readability, pacing, and genre signals.

answer.text: C. Only teachers can decide line breaks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Writers make purposeful formatting choices. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: D. Publication formatting means rewriting the whole piece.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It often means preparing the existing piece for readers.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q20

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which final check best supports clarity, cohesion, and conventions?

answer.text: A. Only check the last word.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The whole piece needs a final pass.

answer.text: B. Trust that spellcheck catches everything.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Spellcheck can miss wrong-word errors. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: C. Read one sentence, line, or script beat at a time to catch distracting errors.

feedback.text: Correct. Slow checking helps identify issues that affect reader understanding.

answer.text: D. Add longer words to sound formal.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Longer words do not automatically improve clarity.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q21

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which formatting choice best supports a poem's pacing?

answer.text: A. Break every word into separate letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Random breaks distract from meaning. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: B. Remove all stanza breaks because poems should be crowded.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Stanza breaks can guide movement. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: C. Use paragraph indentation for every line without purpose.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Format choices should support the poem. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: D. Put an important final phrase on its own line when the pause supports meaning.

feedback.text: Correct. A purposeful line break can slow the reader and emphasize the moment.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q22

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

What should a writer do if the digital preview shows broken spacing?

answer.text: A. Ignore it because the draft looked fine earlier.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The preview shows what the reader may see.

answer.text: B. Fix the spacing and preview again before submission.

feedback.text: Correct. This confirms the reader-facing version is ready.

answer.text: C. Submit a screenshot instead of the assignment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The assignment requires the correct final file.

answer.text: D. Add a note telling readers to imagine the spacing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The final version should display correctly. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q23

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which response best explains online collaborative publication?

answer.text: A. Writing is prepared so others can access, read, and respond to it in a shared digital space.

feedback.text: Correct. Online publication requires reader access and readiness.

answer.text: B. Writing is hidden so no one can read it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Publication means the work is made available to readers.

answer.text: C. Writing is submitted with no title and no format.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Reader access requires preparation. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: D. Writing is changed into a spreadsheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The format should fit the genre and assignment.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q24

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which mistake would most likely lower publication quality?

answer.text: A. Using consistent paragraphing in a story.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That supports readability. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: B. Leaving unresolved comments, random spacing, and a missing title in the final file.

feedback.text: Correct. These issues make the piece look unfinished and harder to read.

answer.text: C. Previewing the file before submission.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Previewing improves readiness. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

answer.text: D. Explaining a purposeful formatting choice.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That supports mastery. This choice is not supported by the provided context or lesson skill; choose the option grounded in the prompt.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: CW_U06_L05_Q25

MLA Standard: MLA.CW.PUB.02

Which final submission choice is best?

answer.text: A. Submit only a rough outline with no title.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The checkpoint requires a publication-ready piece.

answer.text: B. Submit every draft without identifying the final version.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reader needs the intended final version.

answer.text: C. Submit the final formatted piece and a note explaining how format supports the reader.

feedback.text: Correct. This shows both publication readiness and craft reasoning.

answer.text: D. Submit a file with draft comments still visible.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Draft comments usually need to be removed from final publication.
